nodes.label: Network Layer Control Plane
nodes.author: Jim Kurose, Keith Ross
nodes.rationale: Chapter 5 of Kurose and Ross, Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach, 9th edition (Pearson, 2025), covers routing algorithms, OSPF, BGP, SDN controllers, ICMP, and SNMP/NETCONF/YANG.

nodes.label: Per-Router Control Plane
nodes.author: Jim Kurose, Keith Ross
nodes.rationale: Traditional structure in which a routing-algorithm component in every router interacts with other routers to compute that router's forwarding table.

nodes.label: SDN Control Plane
nodes.author: Jim Kurose, Keith Ross
nodes.rationale: Logically centralized control: a remote controller computes and installs forwarding tables. Motivated by easier management, flexible traffic flows, centralized programming of tables, and an open non-proprietary control plane.

nodes.label: Routing
nodes.author: Jim Kurose, Keith Ross
nodes.rationale: Control-plane function that determines the route packets take from source to destination, seeking a good path such as least cost, fastest, or least congested.

nodes.label: Forwarding
nodes.author: Jim Kurose, Keith Ross
nodes.rationale: Data-plane function that moves a packet from a router's input to the appropriate output using values in the arriving packet header.

nodes.label: Link-State Routing
nodes.author: Jim Kurose, Keith Ross
nodes.rationale: Global algorithm: every router has the complete topology and link costs, obtained by link-state broadcast, and computes its own forwarding table. A router can advertise an incorrect link cost, but each router computes only its own table.

nodes.label: Distance-Vector Routing
nodes.author: Jim Kurose, Keith Ross
nodes.rationale: Decentralized, iterative, and asynchronous: each router starts knowing only neighbor link costs, exchanges distance-vector estimates with neighbors, and notifies neighbors only when its vector changes. Errors, including a false low-cost path, can black-hole traffic and propagate.

nodes.label: Dijkstra's Algorithm
nodes.author: Jim Kurose, Keith Ross
nodes.rationale: Iterative least-cost algorithm from one source. After k iterations the least-cost path to k destinations is known. Complexity is O(n^2), with O(n log n) implementations possible; link-state dissemination is also O(n^2). Oscillations are possible when link costs depend on traffic volume. Ties may be broken arbitrarily.

nodes.label: Bellman-Ford Equation
nodes.author: Jim Kurose, Keith Ross
nodes.rationale: Dynamic-programming basis of distance-vector routing: Dx(y) = min over neighbors v of cx,v + Dv(y). The neighbor achieving the minimum is the next hop.

nodes.label: Count-to-Infinity Problem
nodes.author: Jim Kurose, Keith Ross
nodes.rationale: Bad news travels slowly in distance-vector routing. After a link-cost increase, neighbors repeatedly adopt each other's stale path and increment the cost one hop at a time, forming a routing loop. Good news (a cost decrease) converges quickly.

nodes.label: Autonomous System
nodes.author: Jim Kurose, Keith Ross
nodes.rationale: Routers are aggregated into regions (autonomous systems, or domains) because a flat Internet cannot store every destination or flood every route, and each network administration wants to control routing inside its own network.

nodes.label: Intra-AS Routing
nodes.author: Jim Kurose, Keith Ross
nodes.rationale: Routing among routers inside one AS. All routers in an AS run the same intra-domain protocol; different ASes may run different ones. A single administrator makes policy less important than performance.

nodes.label: Inter-AS Routing
nodes.author: Jim Kurose, Keith Ross
nodes.rationale: Routing among ASes. Policy dominates performance: an administration wants control over how its traffic is routed and who routes through its network. Hierarchy also reduces table size and update traffic.

nodes.label: Gateway Router
nodes.author: Jim Kurose, Keith Ross
nodes.rationale: Router at the edge of its AS with links to routers in other ASes. It runs inter-domain routing as well as intra-domain routing, and learns which external destinations are reachable through which neighboring AS.

nodes.label: RIP
nodes.author: Jim Kurose, Keith Ross
nodes.rationale: Routing Information Protocol, a classic distance-vector intra-AS protocol that exchanges distance vectors every 30 seconds. No longer widely used.

nodes.label: EIGRP
nodes.author: Jim Kurose, Keith Ross
nodes.rationale: Enhanced Interior Gateway Routing Protocol, a distance-vector intra-AS protocol. It was Cisco-proprietary for decades and became open in 2013.

nodes.label: OSPF
nodes.author: Jim Kurose, Keith Ross
nodes.rationale: Open Shortest Path First: a publicly available link-state intra-AS protocol. Each router floods link-state advertisements directly over IP, not TCP or UDP, may use bandwidth or delay as link cost, and runs Dijkstra. All OSPF messages are authenticated to prevent malicious intrusion.

nodes.label: IS-IS
nodes.author: Jim Kurose, Keith Ross
nodes.rationale: ISO link-state intra-AS protocol, not an RFC standard, described as essentially the same as OSPF.

nodes.label: Hierarchical OSPF
nodes.author: Jim Kurose, Keith Ross
nodes.rationale: Two-level hierarchy of local areas and a backbone. Link-state advertisements are flooded only inside an area or the backbone, so a router has detailed topology only for its area. Area border routers summarize distances; backbone routers run OSPF on the backbone; boundary routers connect to other ASes.

nodes.label: BGP
nodes.author: Jim Kurose, Keith Ross
nodes.rationale: Border Gateway Protocol, the de facto inter-domain routing protocol and the glue that holds the Internet together. It is a path-vector protocol: peers advertise prefix reachability over a semi-permanent TCP session. Import and export policy decide which paths are accepted and advertised. A typical policy is that an ISP carries traffic to and from its customers and does not provide transit between other ISPs.

nodes.label: eBGP
nodes.author: Jim Kurose, Keith Ross
nodes.rationale: External BGP sessions between gateway routers in neighboring ASes, used to obtain destination-prefix reachability and to advertise reachability onward.

nodes.label: iBGP
nodes.author: Jim Kurose, Keith Ross
nodes.rationale: Internal BGP sessions that propagate reachability learned from neighboring ASes to all routers inside the AS. Gateway routers run both eBGP and iBGP.

nodes.label: AS-PATH
nodes.author: Jim Kurose, Keith Ross
nodes.rationale: BGP route attribute listing the ASes through which a prefix advertisement has passed. Shortest AS-PATH is the second BGP route-selection criterion, after local preference.

nodes.label: NEXT-HOP
nodes.author: Jim Kurose, Keith Ross
nodes.rationale: BGP route attribute identifying the specific internal-AS router that is the next hop toward the next AS. Closest NEXT-HOP is the third route-selection criterion.

nodes.label: Local Preference
nodes.author: Jim Kurose, Keith Ross
nodes.rationale: BGP route attribute used first in route selection. It encodes a policy decision and outranks shortest AS-PATH and hot-potato next hop.

nodes.label: Hot Potato Routing
nodes.author: Jim Kurose, Keith Ross
nodes.rationale: When several local gateways can reach a prefix, choose the gateway with the least intra-domain cost and ignore inter-domain cost, even if that path has more AS hops.

nodes.label: BGP Route Selection
nodes.author: Jim Kurose, Keith Ross
nodes.rationale: When more than one route to a destination is known, select in order: local preference (policy), shortest AS-PATH, closest NEXT-HOP (hot potato), then additional criteria.

nodes.label: BGP Messages
nodes.author: Jim Kurose, Keith Ross
nodes.rationale: Peers exchange OPEN (open the TCP session and authenticate), UPDATE (advertise or withdraw a path), KEEPALIVE (hold the session and ACK OPEN), and NOTIFICATION (report errors and close the connection).

nodes.label: OpenFlow
nodes.author: Jim Kurose, Keith Ross
nodes.rationale: Protocol between an SDN controller and a switch, carried over TCP with optional encryption. Message classes are controller-to-switch, asynchronous switch-to-controller, and symmetric. Distinct from the OpenFlow API, which specifies generalized forwarding actions. Controller-to-switch messages include features, configure, modify-state, and packet-out; switch-to-controller messages include packet-in, flow-removed, and port status.

nodes.label: SDN Controller
nodes.author: Jim Kurose, Keith Ross
nodes.rationale: Network operating system that maintains network state, talks to control applications above and to switches below, and is implemented as a distributed system for performance, scalability, fault tolerance, and robustness. Its layers are device communication, network-wide state management, and an interface for control apps.

nodes.label: Northbound API
nodes.author: Jim Kurose, Keith Ross
nodes.rationale: Interface by which the SDN controller exposes abstractions to network-control applications above it. Examples include a RESTful API and an intent interface.

nodes.label: Southbound API
nodes.author: Jim Kurose, Keith Ross
nodes.rationale: Interface by which the SDN controller communicates with network switches below it. It defines what in the switch is controllable.

nodes.label: ONOS
nodes.author: Jim Kurose, Keith Ross
nodes.rationale: Early influential open-source SDN controller. Control apps are separate from the controller. An intent framework specifies a service as what rather than how. A distributed core emphasizes reliability, replication, and scaling. Southbound protocols include OpenFlow, NETCONF, and OVSDB; northbound abstractions include REST and intent.

nodes.label: ODL
nodes.author: Jim Kurose, Keith Ross
nodes.rationale: Named with ONOS as a practical SDN controller implementation. The slides list it in the chapter goals and summary and do not describe its internals.

nodes.label: Google ORION
nodes.author: Jim Kurose, Keith Ross
nodes.rationale: Google's SDN control plane (NSDI 2021) for the Jupiter datacenter network and the B4 WAN. Intradomain routing, iBGP, and traffic engineering run as applications on the ORION core. Edge-to-edge flow controls such as CoFlow scheduling meet contract SLAs. The core uses pub-sub distributed microservices, and OpenFlow is used for switch signaling and monitoring. ORION provides intradomain services inside Google's network. Amin Vahdat's argument is that configuring a logical network in one controller is simpler than letting every element learn its role from neighbors.

nodes.label: Traffic Engineering
nodes.author: Jim Kurose, Keith Ross
nodes.rationale: With destination-based link-state and distance-vector routing, link weights are the only control knobs. An operator cannot force a specific path, split traffic across two paths, or treat two traffic classes differently without a new algorithm. Generalized forwarding and SDN can realize any desired routing.

nodes.label: ICMP
nodes.author: Jim Kurose, Keith Ross
nodes.rationale: Internet Control Message Protocol, used by hosts and routers for network-level information. Messages are carried in IP datagrams and contain a type, a code, and the first 8 bytes of the datagram that caused the error. Uses include error reporting (unreachable network, host, protocol, or port) and echo request/reply used by ping. Type 11 code 0 is TTL expired; type 3 code 3 is port unreachable. Source quench (type 4 code 0) is unused.

nodes.label: Traceroute
nodes.author: Jim Kurose, Keith Ross
nodes.rationale: Source sends UDP probes with increasing TTL. Each router that expires the TTL returns ICMP type 11 code 0, and the source records RTTs. The destination returns ICMP port unreachable (type 3 code 3), which stops the trace.

nodes.label: Network Management
nodes.author: Jim Kurose, Keith Ross
nodes.rationale: Deployment, integration, and coordination of hardware, software, and people to monitor, test, poll, configure, analyze, evaluate, and control network resources so real-time performance and QoS are met at reasonable cost. Components are a managing server, managed devices with agents, device data, and a management protocol. Operator approaches include CLI, SNMP/MIB, and NETCONF/YANG.

nodes.label: SNMP
nodes.author: Jim Kurose, Keith Ross
nodes.rationale: Simple Network Management Protocol. A managing server queries and sets device data in a MIB. Modes are request/response and trap. Message types are GetRequest, GetNextRequest, GetBulkRequest, SetRequest, Response, and Trap.

nodes.label: MIB
nodes.author: Jim Kurose, Keith Ross
nodes.rationale: Management Information Base: a device's operational and some configuration data, organized as a MIB module. About 400 MIB modules are defined in RFCs, plus many vendor-specific modules. UDP examples include UDPInDatagrams and udpTable, identified by object IDs under 1.3.6.1.2.1.7.

nodes.label: SMI
nodes.author: Jim Kurose, Keith Ross
nodes.rationale: Structure of Management Information, the data-definition language for SNMP MIB variables.

nodes.label: NETCONF
nodes.author: Jim Kurose, Keith Ross
nodes.rationale: Network-wide configuration protocol between a managing server and managed devices. It retrieves, sets, modifies, and activates configuration, supports atomic commit across devices, queries operational data, and subscribes to notifications. Messages are XML RPCs over a secure transport such as TLS. Operations include get-config, get, edit-config, lock, unlock, create-subscription, and notification. A session starts with hello and ends with close-session.

nodes.label: YANG
nodes.author: Jim Kurose, Keith Ross
nodes.rationale: Data-modeling language for the structure, syntax, and semantics of NETCONF management data. It has built-in types like SMI, can generate XML describing a device, and can express constraints that a valid configuration must satisfy.

nodes.label: RFC 2328
nodes.rationale: Cited as the OSPF specification.

nodes.label: RFC 1723
nodes.rationale: Cited as the RIP specification.

nodes.label: RFC 7868
nodes.rationale: Cited for EIGRP becoming an open protocol in 2013.

nodes.label: RFC 4371
nodes.rationale: Cited by the slides for BGP messages OPEN, UPDATE, KEEPALIVE, and NOTIFICATION.
